props.title: The Princess Comes Across
props.initialSlug: A royal romance on the high seas!

sections.content: The Princess Comes Across stands as a fascinating hybrid of romantic comedy and murder mystery, showcasing Carole Lombard's versatility as she plays a Brooklyn actress masquerading as a Swedish princess aboard an ocean liner. The film cleverly plays with the persona of Greta Garbo, as Lombard's character deliberately mimics Garbo's accent and mannerisms. This followed Lombard's breakthrough in Twentieth Century (1934) and came just before her iconic role in My Man Godfrey (1936), representing a peak period in her screwball comedy career.

sections.content: The film's ocean liner setting places it in a notable tradition of 1930s shipboard romances and mysteries, including Transatlantic (1931) and China Seas (1935). Director William K. Howard deftly balances the romantic comedy elements with genuine thriller moments, creating tension through the blackmail subplot while maintaining the light touch necessary for the central romance between Lombard and Fred MacMurray, their second pairing after Hands Across the Table (1935).

The murder mystery aspect of The Princess Comes Across draws from the popular detective fiction of the era, featuring a collection of international sleuths that gently parodies characters like Charlie Chan and Hercule Poirot. This blend of genres was characteristic of Paramount's mid-1930s output, which often combined glamorous settings with elements of mystery, as seen in The Big Broadcast of 1936 (1935) and Desire (1936). movies.title: True Confession
movies.slug: Lombard and MacMurray reunite in this comedy about a pathological liar who confesses to a murder

sections.content: The chemistry between Lombard and MacMurray proved so successful that they would go on to make four films together, including Swing High, Swing Low (1937) and True Confession (1937). Their pairing represented a different dynamic from the screwball battles of Lombard and William Powell in My Man Godfrey (1936), offering a more grounded romantic rapport that balanced comedy with genuine warmth.
